idiom_name: context.WithDeadline/AfterFunc on the message's absolute expiry
implementation_notes: Go's answer is to carry the deadline with the work instead of a TTL in a struct: parse the message's absolute expiry into a time.Time and derive context.WithDeadline (or WithTimeout), so the whole call tree - and every ctx-aware I/O - stops when the message goes stale, while context.AfterFunc schedules the cleanup or dead-letter step that must run on expiry. The derived cancel function is what keeps the runtime timer from leaking, so it is always deferred. This replaces the classic broker-TTL role for in-process work - a context cannot be serialized, so when messages leave the process the TTL is still declared on the transport (the AMQP expiration property) and the context deadline acts as the consumer-side second check.
pitfalls: Context deadlines are only honoured by code that checks ctx or uses ctx-aware calls; a handler that ignores the context keeps running, so pair it with the explicit time.Now().After(expiry) check.
Every derived context in a long-lived consumer must be cancelled; forgetting the deferred cancel leaks the timer and the parent reference until the deadline fires.
A context deadline does not survive serialization: re-stamp the next hop's headers (or publish the broker expiration property) or the message arrives unbounded.
